title: HTTP, HTTPS & DNS
tagline: How browsers turn a URL into pixels — DNS resolution, HTTP request-response, TLS handshake, REST conventions, and WebSockets.

sections.content:
Every time you type a URL and press Enter, an invisible symphony plays out in the background. Before a single byte of HTML or JSON lands in your browser, your operating system must translate a human-readable name like `api.example.com` into a numeric IP address. Then a TCP connection is opened, a cryptographic handshake negotiates a shared secret, and an HTTP request travels across the public internet — all before you see the first character of a response. This chain is so fast and so reliable that we take it for granted, yet it underpins every website, REST API, and mobile app backend you will ever build.

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer protocol that defines how clients and servers exchange requests and responses. It is stateless by design — each request carries all the information needed to process it independently, which is what makes HTTP services easy to scale horizontally. **HTTPS** is HTTP layered on top of **TLS** (Transport Layer Security), which provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Without TLS, anyone on the same network could read or tamper with your traffic. **DNS** (Domain Name System) is the distributed global directory that maps hostnames to IP addresses — a critical piece of infrastructure that most developers interact with daily yet rarely think about deeply.

Understanding these three systems is not merely academic. You will use this knowledge to debug mysterious timeouts (often a DNS caching issue), explain why CORS preflight requests exist (a consequence of HTTP's security model), choose the right status codes for your API (affecting client retry logic and CDN caching), and configure TLS correctly so that browsers do not show scary security warnings to your users. This chapter builds each layer from first principles, then shows how they compose into the full stack you use every day.

sections.title: DNS as a Hierarchical Phone Book with Sticky Notes
sections.content:
Imagine you want to call someone named Alice who works at Acme Corp, but you only know the company name. You call a **Directory Assistance** operator — this is your **recursive resolver**, the intermediary who does the legwork on your behalf.

The operator does not personally know every phone number in the world, so they start at the top. They call the **Country Headquarters** — the **root nameserver** — who says 'I do not have Acme Corp's number, but companies in this country register with the Business Directory.' The operator calls the **Business Directory** — the **TLD nameserver** for `.com` — who says 'Acme Corp has their own internal directory service, here is its number.' The operator calls **Acme Corp's internal directory** — the **authoritative nameserver** — who finally says 'Alice is at extension 34, and that number is valid for the next hour.'

The operator writes Alice's number on a **sticky note** with an expiry time — this is the **TTL (Time To Live)**. The next time someone asks for Alice's number within that hour, the operator reads from the sticky note without repeating the entire chain. This is DNS **caching**. When Alice changes offices (the server changes IP), the old sticky notes must expire before the new number propagates everywhere — this is why DNS changes can take time to 'propagate' globally, sometimes hours if TTL was set high.

sections.title: DNS: The Internet's Distributed Directory
sections.content:
DNS is a **hierarchical, delegated, distributed** database. No single server knows all the answers; instead, authority is divided across millions of nameservers organized in a tree structure that mirrors the domain name hierarchy itself.

**The hierarchy from top to bottom:**

At the apex are the **root nameservers** — there are 13 root server identities (`a.root-servers.net` through `m.root-servers.net`, each with an IPv4 and an IPv6 address), run by 12 organisations and served via **anycast** from nearly 2,000 instances worldwide. They know only one thing: which nameservers are responsible for each top-level domain (TLD) like `.com`, `.org`, `.io`, `.uk`.

**TLD nameservers** are operated by registry organisations — Verisign runs `.com` and `.net`, for example. They store **NS records** (nameserver records) pointing to the authoritative nameservers for each registered domain under their TLD.

**Authoritative nameservers** are the final authority for a specific domain. When you buy `example.com` and configure it with Cloudflare, AWS Route 53, or your registrar, those become the authoritative servers. They hold the actual records: `A` records mapping the domain to an IPv4 address, `AAAA` records for IPv6, `CNAME` aliases, `MX` records for mail, `TXT` records for verification and email security (SPF, DKIM), and more.

**The recursive resolver** (also called a recursor or full-service resolver) is typically provided by your ISP, your corporate network, or a public service like `8.8.8.8` (Google) or `1.1.1.1` (Cloudflare). It handles the iterative queries down the hierarchy on your behalf and caches the results — including the referrals, so in practice it almost never needs to ask a root server: the `.com` servers' addresses are already cached. Your OS's stub resolver simply sends a query to this resolver and waits for a complete answer.

**TTL and propagation:** Every DNS record has a TTL in seconds. A TTL of 3600 means resolvers cache the answer for one hour. Lowering TTL to 60 seconds before changing an IP lets changes propagate within a minute globally; forgetting to lower it first means your old IP could be served from caches for hours after you update the authoritative record.

sequenceDiagram

    participant Root as Root NS (13 clusters)

    participant Auth as Auth NS (example.com)
    R->>Root: Who handles .com?
    Root-->>R: TLD NS IPs for .com
    R->>TLD: Who handles example.com?

sections.title: DNS Record Types in Practice
sections.content:
**A record** — Maps a hostname to a single IPv4 address. You can have multiple A records for the same name (round-robin load balancing at the DNS level). Example: `api.example.com → 93.184.216.34`.

**AAAA record** — Same as A, but for IPv6 addresses (`2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946`). Dual-stack clients usually ask for both A and AAAA, then race IPv6 and IPv4 connection attempts — the **Happy Eyeballs** algorithm (RFC 8305) — so a broken IPv6 path never stalls the user.

**CNAME record** — Canonical name alias. `www.example.com CNAME example.com` means 'resolve `www.example.com` by looking up `example.com`.' CNAMEs cannot coexist with other records at the same name — this is a common trap when trying to use a CNAME at the zone apex (root of the domain). Many DNS providers solve this with a proprietary 'ALIAS' or 'ANAME' flattening record.

**MX record** — Mail exchanger. Specifies which server receives email for a domain, along with a **priority** (lower = preferred). `example.com MX 10 mail.example.com, 20 backup-mail.example.com`.

**TXT record** — Arbitrary text. The Swiss Army knife of DNS: used for **SPF** (specifying which servers may send email as your domain), **DKIM** (public key for email signing), **DMARC** (email authentication policy), and domain ownership verification by services like Google Search Console.

**NS record** — Delegates a zone (or subdomain) to specific nameservers. The NS records at the TLD level are what make the DNS hierarchy work — they tell resolvers 'for anything under `example.com`, ask these nameservers.'

**SOA record** — Start of Authority. One per zone; contains zone metadata including the primary nameserver, admin email, serial number (incremented on every change to trigger zone transfers), and default TTL values.

**SRV record** — Service location. `_http._tcp.example.com SRV 0 5 80 www.example.com` specifies the host and port for a service. Used by SIP, XMPP, and some service-discovery protocols, though most web services have moved to environment variables or service meshes instead.

**HTTPS / SVCB records** (RFC 9460, 2023) — tell clients *before they connect* which protocols a service supports (`alpn="h3,h2"`), alternative endpoints and ports, and Encrypted ClientHello keys. Browsers use them to go straight to HTTP/3, and they offer a standard way to alias a zone apex.

**CAA record** — lists which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain; CAs must check it before issuing.

**PTR record** — reverse DNS: maps an IP address back to a name (under `in-addr.arpa` / `ip6.arpa`). Mail servers check it when filtering spam.

sections.title: DNS in Practice: Caching Layers, Transport and Privacy
sections.content:
**Caching happens at every layer**: the browser keeps its own short-lived cache, the OS stub resolver has one (`systemd-resolved` on Linux, `mDNSResponder` on macOS), so may the home router, and the recursive resolver caches for everyone behind it. Negative answers are cached too: an `NXDOMAIN` is remembered for the time given in the zone's SOA record, so a hostname looked up *before* you created it can keep failing for a while.

**Transport**: classic DNS uses UDP port 53 with a 512-byte answer limit. EDNS(0) lets clients advertise a larger buffer (about 1,232 bytes is the recommended safe size, to avoid IP fragmentation); if an answer still does not fit, the server sets the TC (truncated) bit and the client retries over TCP.

**Privacy and integrity**: plain DNS is unencrypted and unauthenticated — anyone on the path can see, and spoof, your lookups. **DNS over HTTPS (DoH)** and **DNS over TLS (DoT)** encrypt the hop from client to resolver (browsers, Android, iOS and Windows support them), while **DNSSEC** signs records so a validating resolver can prove they came from the zone owner. They solve different problems: DoH hides queries from the network; DNSSEC proves answers are authentic.

**A Node.js gotcha**: `dns.lookup()` — what `http`, `net` and `fetch` use by default — calls the OS resolver (`getaddrinfo`) on libuv's 4-thread pool and honours `/etc/hosts`, while `dns.resolve*()` sends real DNS queries over the network. Many slow lookups can saturate that thread pool and delay unrelated file-system and crypto work.

sections.title: HTTP: The Request-Response Protocol
sections.content:
HTTP was designed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 and first formalised as HTTP/1.0 in 1996. It is a **stateless, application-layer** protocol — text-based and carried over TCP in its first versions. 'Stateless' is a deliberate design choice: each HTTP request stands alone, carrying all the context needed to process it. This makes HTTP services horizontally scalable — any server that handles `GET /users/42` can serve the same request, because no server-side session is required.

**An HTTP request has three parts:**

1. **Request line** — method, path, and HTTP version. Example: `GET /api/users/42 HTTP/1.1`
2. **Headers** — key-value metadata. `Host: api.example.com`, `Authorization: Bearer eyJ...`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `Accept: application/json`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`.
3. **Body** — optional payload, present for POST/PUT/PATCH. The `Content-Type` header tells the server how to parse it.

**An HTTP response similarly has three parts:**

1. **Status line** — HTTP version, numeric status code, reason phrase. Example: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`
2. **Headers** — `Content-Type: application/json`, `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`, `ETag: "abc123"`, `Set-Cookie: session=...`
3. **Body** — the response payload (HTML, JSON, binary).

The semantics — methods, status codes, headers — have stayed the same since HTTP/1.1. What changed across versions is the wire format and the transport underneath, covered next.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["HTTP Request"] --> B["Request Line\nGET /api/users HTTP/1.1"]
    A --> C["Headers\nHost, Auth, Content-Type"]
    A --> D["Body\nJSON / form data (optional)"]
    E["HTTP Response"] --> F["Status Line\nHTTP/1.1 200 OK"]
    E --> G["Headers\nContent-Type, Cache-Control, ETag"]
    E --> H["Body\nJSON / HTML / binary"]
sections.caption: Structure of HTTP request and response — each message is a status line, headers, and an optional body.

sections.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
sections.content:
**HTTP/1.1** (1997; current spec RFC 9112) is text-based. Connections are persistent (keep-alive), but each connection carries one request at a time — pipelining was specified but never usable in practice — so browsers open up to **six connections per origin**, and a slow response blocks the requests queued behind it (*HTTP-level head-of-line blocking*).

**HTTP/2** (2015, RFC 9113) keeps the same semantics but sends binary **frames** over a single TCP connection. Many requests travel as interleaved **streams**, headers are compressed with **HPACK**, and one connection per origin is enough. This removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking — but not *TCP's*: one lost packet stalls every stream until it is retransmitted, so on lossy networks HTTP/2 can do worse than several HTTP/1.1 connections. (Server push was specified, but browsers have since removed support for it.)

**HTTP/3** (2022, RFC 9114) maps the same semantics onto **QUIC** over UDP. Streams are independent at the transport layer, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream; TLS 1.3 is built in, a new connection is ready in 1 RTT (0-RTT on resumption), and connection IDs let a phone move from Wi-Fi to cellular without reconnecting. Header compression is **QPACK**. By 2025–26 HTTP/3 is on by default in all major browsers and CDNs. Clients learn that a server speaks it from an `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` response header or an HTTPS DNS record, and fall back to HTTP/2 when UDP is blocked.

| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP | TCP | QUIC over UDP |
| Wire format | Text | Binary frames | Binary frames |
| Requests per connection | One at a time | Many, multiplexed | Many, multiplexed |
| Head-of-line blocking | HTTP and TCP level | TCP level | Per stream only |
| Header compression | None | HPACK | QPACK |
| Encryption | Optional | Required by browsers | Always (TLS 1.3) |
| Round trips before first request (new connection) | 2 with TLS 1.3 | 2 with TLS 1.3 | 1 |

sections.title: HTTP Methods: Semantics Matter
sections.content:
HTTP defines a small set of **methods** (also called verbs) that encode the intended action. Using them correctly is not ceremony — caches, proxies, browsers, and REST clients all make decisions based on method semantics.

**GET** — Retrieve a resource. **Safe** (no side effects on the server) and **idempotent** (repeating it gives the same result). Browsers cache GET responses; proxies may too. Never put sensitive data in a GET URL — it ends up in server logs, browser history, and referrer headers.

**POST** — Submit data to create a resource or trigger an action. **Not safe**, **not idempotent** — submitting a form twice may create two records. POST bodies carry the payload; POST responses typically return `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource.

**PUT** — Replace a resource in its entirety. **Idempotent** — putting the same document twice results in the same state as putting it once. If you want `PUT /users/42` to update only the name, you must send the full user object, not just the name field.

**PATCH** — Partial update. Only send the fields you want to change. Not guaranteed idempotent by the spec (the patch document could describe relative changes like 'increment counter by 1'), but implementations that use it for simple field updates treat it as idempotent in practice.

**DELETE** — Remove a resource. Idempotent — the server state after one DELETE or ten is the same: the resource is gone. The *response* may differ (`204` the first time, `404` afterwards), so a client retrying a DELETE should treat `404` as success. Returns `204 No Content` on success typically.

**HEAD** — Same as GET but without the response body. Useful to check `Content-Length`, `Last-Modified`, or `ETag` before deciding whether to download a large file. Efficient health checks and cache validation use HEAD.

**OPTIONS** — Describe the allowed methods for a resource. Browsers send **CORS preflight** requests using OPTIONS when a cross-origin request uses a method other than GET, HEAD or POST, sets headers outside the CORS-safelisted set (such as `Authorization`), or sends a `Content-Type` other than `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` — so an ordinary JSON `POST` is preflighted. The browser first asks "is this allowed?" before sending the actual request.

**Idempotency is critical for retry logic.** If a GET, PUT, or DELETE times out, you can safely retry it — you know it will produce the same result as one successful call. If a POST times out, retrying may create duplicate resources — you need idempotency keys or deduplication on the server side.

sections.title: HTTP Status Codes: Load-Bearing Metadata
sections.content:
Status codes are not cosmetic — they drive behaviour in clients, proxies, CDNs, and load balancers. Using the wrong code is a bug, not a stylistic choice.

**2xx — Success:** `200 OK` is the standard success for GET and POST. `201 Created` should accompany POST responses that create a new resource, and should include a `Location` header with the URL of the new resource. `204 No Content` signals success with no body — appropriate for DELETE and some PATCH operations. `206 Partial Content` is used for byte-range requests (video streaming, resumable downloads).

**3xx — Redirection:** `301 Moved Permanently` tells clients (and search engines) to update their bookmarks — the resource has a new permanent URL. `302 Found` (temporary redirect) is used for transient redirects, like after a POST-redirect-GET pattern. `304 Not Modified` is the cache validation response: 'you already have the current version, use your cached copy.' This saves bandwidth without the client needing to guess. `307 Temporary Redirect` and `308 Permanent Redirect` are modern equivalents of 302/301 that guarantee the method is preserved (a POST to a 307 target stays POST; a POST to a 302 target historically became GET).

**4xx — Client errors:** The client did something wrong. `400 Bad Request` — malformed syntax or invalid parameters. `401 Unauthorized` — authentication required or credentials invalid (despite the name, it means 'unauthenticated'). `403 Forbidden` — authenticated but not permitted. `404 Not Found` — resource does not exist at this path. `405 Method Not Allowed` — the method is not supported on this endpoint. `409 Conflict` — state conflict (trying to create a duplicate, or optimistic locking failure). `422 Unprocessable Content` (called "Unprocessable Entity" before RFC 9110) — syntactically valid but semantically invalid (common in Rails and NestJS for validation failures). `429 Too Many Requests` — rate limit exceeded; should include `Retry-After` header.

**5xx — Server errors:** The server failed. `500 Internal Server Error` — unhandled exception. `502 Bad Gateway` — the upstream server (behind your load balancer or reverse proxy) returned an invalid response. `503 Service Unavailable` — server is overloaded or down for maintenance; include `Retry-After` when possible. `504 Gateway Timeout` — upstream did not respond in time.

A critical distinction: **most 4xx mean do NOT retry without fixing the request** (retrying a 400 will always fail) — the exceptions are `408 Request Timeout` and `429 Too Many Requests`, which should be retried after the `Retry-After` delay. **5xx often means retry with exponential backoff** (except `501 Not Implemented` and `505 HTTP Version Not Supported`, which are not transient) — but retry automatically only for **idempotent** requests. Retrying a POST that timed out or returned `502` may execute it twice unless the server supports idempotency keys.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: `fetch()` only rejects on network-level failures (DNS errors, refused or reset connections, aborts); it resolves for every HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx, so you must check `res.ok` or `res.status`. This wrapper adds the three things production clients need: a timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout`) so a hung server cannot hang the caller, retries with exponential backoff and jitter that honour `Retry-After`, and — most importantly — retries **only** for idempotent methods or requests carrying an `Idempotency-Key`, because blindly retrying a POST can charge a card twice. `408`, `429` and transient 5xx are retried; other 4xx are thrown immediately.

sections.title: TLS: How HTTPS Actually Secures Traffic
sections.content:
TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL) provides three guarantees when you connect to an HTTPS endpoint:

1. **Confidentiality** — traffic is encrypted so eavesdroppers see only ciphertext.
2. **Integrity** — messages are authenticated so tampering is detected.
3. **Authentication** — the server proves its identity via a **certificate** signed by a trusted **Certificate Authority (CA)**.

**How certificates work:** A TLS certificate is a document that binds a public key to a domain name (and other metadata like organisation and expiry date). It is digitally signed by a CA — a company like Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, or Sectigo that browsers and operating systems have agreed to trust. When your browser connects to `https://bank.example.com`, it verifies that the certificate presented covers that domain, is not expired, and is signed by a trusted CA. If any check fails, you see a browser warning.

**The TLS 1.3 handshake (1 round trip):**

- **Client → Server: ClientHello** — 'I support these cipher suites, here is my DH key share.' The client sends its half of the key exchange in the very first message.
- **Server → Client: ServerHello + Certificate + CertificateVerify + Finished** — 'Here is my DH key share' (both sides can now derive the session keys, so everything after ServerHello is already encrypted), 'here is my certificate, a signature proving I hold its private key (CertificateVerify), and a MAC over the whole handshake (Finished).'
- **Client → Server: Finished** — 'I verified your certificate. Let's start talking.' The client sends its first HTTP request right behind it, in the same flight.

At this point, symmetric keys have been established in **one round trip** (one client-to-server message, one server-to-client reply). Symmetric encryption (AES-GCM) is then used for all subsequent HTTP data — it is far faster than asymmetric (RSA/ECDSA) cryptography.

**TLS 1.2 vs 1.3:** TLS 1.2 required two round trips before data could flow. TLS 1.3 eliminated obsolete cipher suites, changed the handshake to one RTT, and added **0-RTT resumption** for previously-visited sites (the client sends data in the first message using a session ticket from the previous connection). However, 0-RTT data has replay attack risks, so it should only be used for idempotent requests.

**Forward secrecy:** TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which means session keys are never stored persistently. Even if someone records all your encrypted traffic and later steals the server's private key, they cannot decrypt the old traffic. This property — called **forward secrecy** or **perfect forward secrecy (PFS)** — is a major improvement over static RSA key exchange, which TLS 1.2 and earlier still allowed (TLS 1.2 with ECDHE cipher suites also has forward secrecy).

**SNI and ECH:** the ClientHello names the site it wants (**Server Name Indication**) so one IP address can serve many certificates — historically in plaintext, visible to anyone on the path. **Encrypted ClientHello (ECH)**, supported by Chrome and Firefox and deployed by Cloudflare, encrypts it with a key published in the site's HTTPS DNS record.

**Post-quantum key exchange:** Chrome, Firefox and the major CDNs now negotiate the hybrid **X25519MLKEM768** group by default, combining classic elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman with the ML-KEM (Kyber) post-quantum scheme, so traffic recorded today stays confidential even against a future quantum computer.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: ClientHello (DH key_share, cipher suites)
    S->>C: ServerHello + Certificate + CertVerify + Finished
    Note over C,S: Both derive symmetric keys from DH exchange
    C->>S: Finished (certificate verified)
    C->>S: GET /api/data (encrypted)
    S->>C: 200 OK + body (encrypted)
sections.caption: TLS 1.3 handshake: one round trip before encrypted HTTP flows. The asymmetric DH exchange derives ephemeral symmetric keys; all data is then encrypted with AES-GCM.

sections.title: HTTPS in Production: The Practical Checklist
sections.content:
Understanding TLS conceptually is one thing; deploying it correctly is another. Here are the operational considerations every developer should know:

**Certificate management:** Let's Encrypt provides free, automatically-renewing 90-day certificates via the ACME protocol. Tools like `certbot` or the `tls-alpn-01` ACME challenge built into Caddy make this nearly automatic. The 90-day lifetime encourages automation — relying on manual renewal is a common source of outages ('the certificate expired over the weekend'). Lifetimes keep shrinking industry-wide: CA/Browser Forum rules cut the maximum lifetime of public certificates to 200 days from March 2026, 100 days in 2027 and 47 days by 2029 — automated renewal is no longer optional.

**TLS termination:** In production, TLS is usually terminated at a **load balancer** or **reverse proxy** (nginx, Caddy, AWS ALB, Cloudflare), not in your application server. The proxy handles TLS, and your app receives plain HTTP from a trusted internal network. This simplifies certificate management and lets you use your application framework without TLS configuration.

**HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security):** The `Strict-Transport-Security` response header tells browsers 'for the next N seconds, always connect to this domain over HTTPS, even if the user types `http://`.' This prevents **SSL stripping attacks** where a man-in-the-middle downgrades an HTTP connection before HTTPS begins. Example: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`.

**Mixed content:** If an HTTPS page loads any resource (image, script, API request) over plain HTTP, the browser blocks or warns. Every resource must be served over HTTPS.

**Certificate pinning:** Mobile apps sometimes pin specific certificates or public keys to prevent attacks using rogue but CA-signed certificates. This is powerful but brittle — if your cert changes, pinned apps break until updated — and it is now generally discouraged; browsers dropped HTTP-header pinning (HPKP) back in 2018.

**Secure cookie flags:** Session cookies must have `Secure` (only sent over HTTPS), `HttpOnly` (not accessible to JavaScript, preventing XSS theft), and `SameSite=Strict` or `Lax` (prevents CSRF attacks). Forgetting any of these flags is a classic security vulnerability.

flowchart LR
    A["Browser"] -->|"HTTPS TLS"| B["Load Balancer / CDN"]
    B -->|"Plain HTTP internal"| C["App Server"]
    C -->|"DB queries"| D["Database"]
    B -.->|"Certificate\n(Let's Encrypt)"| E["ACME CA"]
sections.caption: Typical production HTTPS architecture: TLS terminates at the load balancer or CDN edge; app servers receive plain HTTP from the trusted internal network.

sections.title: WebSockets: Upgrading HTTP to Full-Duplex
sections.content:
HTTP's request-response model means the server can only send data when the client asks. For real-time applications — chat, live dashboards, collaborative editing, stock tickers — polling (repeatedly asking 'any updates?') is wasteful and slow. **WebSockets** solve this by upgrading an HTTP connection to a persistent, **full-duplex** channel where either side can send messages at any time.

**The WebSocket handshake** starts as a normal HTTP request:

```
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: ws.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
```

If the server accepts, it responds with `101 Switching Protocols`:

```
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
```

After `101`, the HTTP protocol is discarded and the connection operates with WebSocket's lightweight binary **framing protocol**. Messages can be text (UTF-8) or binary, and can be split across multiple frames for large payloads.

**WebSockets vs. alternatives:**

- **Long polling** — client sends a request, server holds it open until there is data, then closes it and the client immediately sends another. Works everywhere but wasteful at scale.
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** — server streams one-way events to the client over a persistent HTTP connection. Simpler than WebSockets for push-only use cases (news feeds, log tailing), supports automatic reconnection natively.
- **WebSockets** — true bidirectional. Required when the client also needs to push events (multiplayer games, collaborative editing, real-time trading).

In production, WebSocket connections go through the same TLS (`wss://` instead of `ws://` — always use `wss://`). A WebSocket stays pinned to whichever backend accepted it, so the load balancer must pass the `Upgrade` through and allow long idle timeouts. **Sticky sessions** are only needed when a library falls back to HTTP long-polling (Socket.IO, for example) or when reconnects must land on the same server. Because connections are long-lived, expect uneven load after deploys and design for reconnect storms. When scaling horizontally, you typically need a **pub/sub broker** (Redis, Kafka) to route messages between WebSocket servers.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Production WebSocket clients need three things: exponential backoff reconnection (do not hammer the server with immediate reconnects), heartbeat pings (load balancers with idle connection timeouts will silently drop the connection), and safe send guard (check `readyState === OPEN` before sending). Decide whether to reconnect by *who* closed the socket: reconnect unless the app itself called `close()` — a `1001 Going Away` from the server typically means a deploy. Jitter stops thousands of clients reconnecting in the same instant. The heartbeat is an application-level message because the browser WebSocket API cannot send protocol-level ping frames (servers can, and browsers answer them automatically).

sections.title: REST Design: Conventions and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style, not a protocol. A 'RESTful' API uses HTTP semantics correctly to expose resources. Here are the conventions that matter most:

**URLs identify resources, not actions.** The URL `/users/42/activate` is not RESTful — it encodes an action verb. A RESTful equivalent is `PATCH /users/42` with `{ status: 'active' }` in the body, or `POST /users/42/activations` if activation is a separate resource.

**Collections and singletons follow a pattern.** `GET /users` returns a collection. `POST /users` creates a member. `GET /users/42` returns the member. `PUT /users/42` replaces it. `PATCH /users/42` partially updates it. `DELETE /users/42` removes it. This pattern is predictable — any developer can guess how to interact with a new resource type.

**Use query parameters for filtering and pagination, not path segments.** `GET /users?role=admin&page=2&limit=20` is correct. `GET /admin-users/page/2` is not RESTful.

**Return appropriate status codes.** Returning `200 OK` for every response (including errors) forces clients to inspect the body to detect failures — breaking HTTP client libraries, CDN error detection, and observability tooling.

**Common REST mistakes:**

- Using `GET` for operations that change state ('please `GET /delete-user?id=42`') — this is catastrophically wrong because browsers, search engines, and prefetchers will trigger GET requests without user intent.
- Using `POST` for everything — you lose caching, idempotency semantics, and REST client support.
- Returning `200` with `{ error: true }` in the body — use `4xx/5xx` status codes.
- Nesting resources more than two levels deep (`/users/42/posts/7/comments/3/votes/1`) — flatten the URL space instead (`/votes/1`).
- Not versioning the API — once clients depend on your API shape, breaking changes require versioning (`/api/v2/users`) or content negotiation.

**CORS: Why Browsers Send OPTIONS First**

The **Same-Origin Policy** is a browser security rule: JavaScript on `app.example.com` cannot make requests to `api.otherdomain.com` without permission. **CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** is the mechanism that grants exceptions. For 'simple' requests (GET, HEAD or POST with only CORS-safelisted headers and a form-style or `text/plain` body), the browser sends the request and then checks the response headers. For everything else — PUT, DELETE, an `Authorization` header, a JSON body — the browser first sends an **OPTIONS preflight** request to check permission. Your server must respond to OPTIONS with appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` headers. If the preflight fails, the browser never sends the real request. Simple requests have no preflight: they *are* sent and processed, and the browser merely hides the response from JavaScript — which is why CORS is not a CSRF defence. Browsers refuse to combine `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials (cookies), so the dangerous misconfiguration is reflecting any request `Origin` back together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`: that lets any website make authenticated requests and read the answers. Keep an explicit allow-list of origins.

**Common interview traps and debugging tips:**

- `fetch()` does NOT throw on 4xx or 5xx — it only rejects on network failures. Always check `res.ok` or `res.status`. This trips up almost every developer coming from `axios` or `curl`.
- `401 Unauthorized` means **unauthenticated** (bad/missing credentials); `403 Forbidden` means **unauthorized** (authenticated but not permitted). The naming is historical and counterintuitive.
- DNS TTL lowers must happen BEFORE you change the IP, not after. If TTL is 86400 and you change it to 60 at the same time as the IP, the old TTL (86400) is what caches will respect for the transition window.
- WebSocket connections fail silently through some proxies — if WS is being blocked, try `wss://` on port 443 (TLS), which looks identical to HTTPS traffic to most proxies.
- CNAME records cannot be placed at the zone apex (root domain, e.g., `example.com` itself) — use an ALIAS/ANAME record or an A record instead. Only subdomains can be CNAMEs.
- TLS 1.3's 0-RTT resumption should only be used for idempotent requests such as `GET` — it has replay attack risk for non-idempotent operations.

items: **DNS resolution follows a hierarchy** — recursive resolver queries root → TLD → authoritative nameserver — caching results by TTL. Changing DNS records does not propagate until old cache entries expire; lower TTL to 60 seconds before planned changes.

**HTTP versions** share semantics but not transport: HTTP/1.1 = one request at a time per TCP connection; HTTP/2 = multiplexed streams on one TCP connection (TCP head-of-line blocking remains); HTTP/3 = streams over QUIC/UDP, 1-RTT setup, no cross-stream blocking, discovered via `Alt-Svc` or HTTPS DNS records.

**HTTP methods carry semantics** that clients, caches, and proxies rely on. GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE are idempotent (safe to retry); POST is not. Using the wrong method breaks caching, retry logic, and REST client libraries.

**Status codes are load-bearing** — `2xx` success, `3xx` redirect, `4xx` client fault (do not retry — except 408/429), `5xx` server fault (retry *idempotent* requests with backoff). `fetch()` never throws on 4xx/5xx — always check `res.ok` or `res.status`.

**TLS 1.3** completes the handshake in one round trip using ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange, derives symmetric session keys, and provides forward secrecy — even recording all traffic and stealing the server's private key later cannot decrypt past sessions.

**WebSockets** upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent full-duplex channel via `Upgrade: websocket` and `101 Switching Protocols`. Use reconnection with exponential backoff, heartbeat pings for idle-connection timeouts, and always use `wss://` in production.

**CORS preflight (OPTIONS)** is the browser's permission check before a cross-origin non-simple request. Your server must handle OPTIONS with correct `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers; never reflect arbitrary origins together with `Allow-Credentials: true`.

**HTTPS in production** means TLS termination at the load balancer, automatic certificate renewal (Let's Encrypt), HSTS headers to prevent SSL stripping, and `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite` flags on all session cookies.

**DNS details that bite**: negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too; large answers fall back to TCP; DoH/DoT encrypt lookups while DNSSEC authenticates them; Node's `dns.lookup()` runs on the libuv thread pool.

quiz.question: What does the TTL field in a DNS record control?
options: The time a DNS server waits before timing out a query
How long resolvers and OS caches keep the answer before re-querying
The maximum number of nameservers a query may traverse
The validity period of the TLS certificate for the domain
quiz.explanation: TTL (Time To Live) specifies how many seconds downstream resolvers and OS caches should keep the DNS answer before discarding it and re-querying. A TTL of 3600 means caches hold the answer for one hour. To minimise propagation delay before changing an IP address, lower the TTL to 60 seconds at least one full TTL period before making the change.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is both SAFE and IDEMPOTENT?
options: POST
PUT
DELETE
GET
quiz.explanation: GET is safe (no server-side side effects) and idempotent (repeating it produces the same result). PUT is idempotent but not safe — it modifies state. DELETE is idempotent but not safe. POST is neither safe nor idempotent — repeated POSTs may create duplicate resources.

quiz.question: A client receives HTTP 401. What does this indicate?
options: The resource was not found at this URL
The client is authenticated but lacks the required permission
Authentication is required or the provided credentials were invalid
The server encountered an unhandled internal error
quiz.explanation: 401 Unauthorized (confusingly named) means the request requires authentication — either no credentials were sent, or the credentials were invalid. 403 Forbidden means the client IS authenticated but does not have permission. 404 is not found; 500 is a server error.

quiz.question: How many round trips does TLS 1.3 require before encrypted HTTP data can flow?
options: 0 (data flows in the very first client message for all connections)
1 (ClientHello → ServerHello+Cert+Finished → client Finished)
2 (same as TLS 1.2)
3 (key exchange, certificate verification, and session start)
quiz.explanation: TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in 1 round trip: the client sends ClientHello with a DH key share, the server responds with ServerHello, its certificate, and Finished — both sides can now derive the same symmetric session keys. 0-RTT resumption exists for previously-connected clients but has replay attack risks and is not used for all connections.

quiz.question: What HTTP header does a client include to initiate a WebSocket upgrade?
options: Upgrade: websocket
Content-Type: websocket
Protocol-Switch: websocket
Transfer-Encoding: websocket
quiz.explanation: A WebSocket upgrade request includes 'Upgrade: websocket', 'Connection: Upgrade', and 'Sec-WebSocket-Key' (a random nonce). The server responds with 101 Switching Protocols and 'Sec-WebSocket-Accept' (a derived hash). After 101, both sides communicate using the WebSocket framing protocol instead of HTTP.

quiz.question: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?
options: CNAME
MX
TXT
A
quiz.explanation: An A record maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address (e.g., example.com → 93.184.216.34). AAAA maps to IPv6. CNAME is an alias pointing to another hostname — the resolver follows the chain. MX specifies mail servers. TXT holds arbitrary text for SPF, DKIM, domain ownership proofs, etc.

quiz.question: An HTTP DELETE request returns 204. What should the client do?
options: Retry — 204 indicates partial completion
Parse the empty body for a result object
Treat the request as successful and expect no body
Redirect to the parent collection URL
quiz.explanation: HTTP 204 No Content means the request succeeded and there is intentionally no response body. It is the conventional success code for DELETE and some PATCH operations where returning the resource is unnecessary. The client must not attempt to parse a body — there is none.

quiz.question: Why does fetch() NOT automatically throw an error when the server returns 404?
options: 404 is classified as a successful response in the HTTP specification
fetch() only rejects its Promise on network-level failures, not HTTP error status codes
A plugin or interceptor is required to enable HTTP error detection in fetch()
The response body must be fully read before the status code is available
quiz.explanation: fetch() resolves its Promise for any complete HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx status codes. It only rejects on network-level failures such as DNS resolution failure or connection refused. To detect HTTP errors you must check res.ok (true for 200–299) or res.status and throw manually.

quiz.question: What property does TLS 1.3's use of ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange provide?
options: Zero round-trip resumption for all connections
Symmetric key reuse across multiple sessions for performance
Certificate pinning — the certificate is baked into the client application
Forward secrecy — past sessions cannot be decrypted even if the server private key is later compromised
quiz.explanation: Ephemeral DH key exchange means each session generates a fresh key pair that is discarded after use. Session keys are never stored. Even if an attacker records all encrypted traffic and later obtains the server's private key, they cannot derive the session keys and thus cannot decrypt past sessions. This is called forward secrecy (or perfect forward secrecy, PFS).

quiz.question: In iterative DNS resolution, which server does the recursive resolver query FIRST?
options: The authoritative nameserver for the specific domain
The TLD nameserver (e.g., Verisign's .com servers)
One of the 13 root nameserver clusters
The client's local ISP nameserver cache
quiz.explanation: With a cold cache, iterative resolution starts at the root nameservers — 13 root server identities (a through m) served from nearly 2,000 anycast instances. In practice resolvers cache the TLD referrals, so most lookups skip this step. The root responds with the TLD nameserver addresses for the relevant TLD (.com, .org, etc.), and the resolver then queries the TLD, then the authoritative nameserver for the specific domain.
